blocks.text: The curruca [warbler], in Greek ὑπολαῒς [hypolais], is a small bird in whose nest the cuckoo usually lays. The Philosopher says of the cuckoo, Hist. book 6, ch. 7: τίκτει δὲ ἐπὶ τῇ τῆς ὑπολαΐδος νεοττείᾳ, ἡ δὲ ἐκλέπει, καὶ ἐκτρέφει [tiktei de epi tē tēs hypolaidos neotteia, hē de eklepei, kai ektrephei]. Hence Theophrastus (De caus. plant. book 2, ch. 24) denied that the race of cuckoos could exist εἰ μὴ ἦν ἡ ὑπολαῒς, ἡ καὶ εἰς τὴν νεοττίαν τὰ ὠὰ τίθησιν [ei mē ēn hē hypolais, hē kai eis tēn neottian ta ōa tithēsin], if there were not the warbler, in whose nest it might lay its eggs. This is not entirely true, since besides the warbler there are also other birds in whose nest the cuckoo ὠοτοκεῖ [ōotokei]. Aristotle in the Mirabilia: Τοὺς κόκκυγάς φασι μὴ ποιεῖν νεοττίαν, ἀλλ’ ἐν ταῖς τῶν φαττῶν, καὶ ταῖς τῶν τρυγόνων ἐκτίκτειν [Tous kokkygas phasi mē poiein neottian, all’ en tais tōn phattōn, kai tais tōn trygonōn ektiktein]. Likewise Hist. book 9, ch. 29: Ἐν ἀλλοτρίαις τίκτει νεοττίαις, μάλιστα μὲν ἐν ταῖς τῶν φαβῶν, καὶ ἐν ὑπολαΐδος, καὶ κορύδου χαμαὶ, ἐπὶ δένδρου ἐν τῇ τῆς χλωρίδος καλουμένης νεοττίᾳ [En allotriais tiktei neottiais, malista men en tais tōn phabōn, kai en hypolaidos, kai korydou chamai, epi dendrou en tē tēs chlōridos kaloumenēs neottia]. Antigonus, Mirab. ch. 109: Κόκκυγος δὲ νεοττοὺς οὐδένα ἑωρακέναι. Τίκτειν γὰρ αὐτὸν, οὐκ ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ νεοττίᾳ, ἀλλ’ εἰς τὰς τῶν ὀρνιθίων, ἢ εἰς τὰς τῶν φαβῶν, ἢ ὑποδυσιδέων [Kokkygos de neottous oudena heōrakenai. Tiktein gar auton, ouk en tē idia neottia, all’ eis tas tōn ornithiōn, ē eis tas tōn phabōn, ē hypodysideōn] (read ὑπολαΐδων [hypolaidōn]) εἰσπετόμενον [eispetomenon]. Aelian, Hist. book 3, ch. 30: Οὐ πάντων δὲ ὀρνίθων καλίαις ἐπιπηδᾷ οὗτός γε, ἀλλὰ κορύδου, καὶ φάττης, καὶ χλωρίδος, καὶ πάππου [Ou pantōn de ornithōn kaliais epipēda houtos ge, alla korydou, kai phattēs, kai chlōridos, kai pappou]. You see, reader, that besides the warbler, the wood pigeon, the turtle dove, [II, 644] the lark, the chloris and the pappus are also counted among the birds whose nests the cuckoo invades. Some add the sparrow. Isidore, book 12, ch. 7, on the cuckoo: It eats the sparrow's eggs found in the nest and puts its own in their place, which the sparrow takes up, incubates and rears. And Gesner adds the nightingale as well, and the wagtail, the robin and the redstart. So these are so many birds that brood what they did not lay. To them may be added from Jeremiah the bird קרא kore, different from all these and closer to the σκολόπαξ [skolopax] or woodcock (rusticula), as we have proved. This could not be observed by the Greeks and Romans, because this bird was unknown to them. And it escaped the Arabs too, because they touch on its description only briefly and lightly.

But, you will say, if קרא kore is a species of σκολόπαξ [skolopax] or woodcock, or a bird very similar to it, why do the Greek, Latin, Syriac, Arabic and Hebrew translators render it partridge with such agreement? Two answers can be given. 1. The Greeks, who preceded all these, [col. 89] took קרא kore, with Koph, and כרא cara, with Caph, indiscriminately; and the latter means partridge among the Arabs even today. So it is written in Giggeius; others prefer كري [karī], and كروان [karawān]. Alcamus: الكروان الحجل والقبج والانثي الكروانة ويقال للذكر الكري [al-karawān al-ḥajal wa-l-qabj wa-l-unthī al-karawāna wa-yuqāl li-l-dhakar al-karī] Alcarvvan, the male partridge, and the partridge in general; and the female alcarvana. But the male is also called alcara ^{(5)}. In Ezech. VII, 25. קפדה־בא, destruction comes, was rendered by the Greeks ἐξιλασμὸς ἥξει [exilasmos hēxei], propitiation will come, as if קפדה with Koph and Daleth were the same as כפרה with Caph and Resh. In the same way קרא with Koph could have been taken for כרא. 2. Moreover, some think the σκολόπαξ [skolopax] is a species of partridge, because, although it differs not a little from the partridge in form and appearance, it comes close to it in taste. Hence in Martial the woodcock boasts thus:
Am I a woodcock or a partridge? What does it matter, if the taste is the same?

And this is confirmed by all who call the σκολόπαξ [skolopax] rustica or rusticula, as Pliny, book 10, ch. 38: Some (birds) run, like partridges and woodcocks. For they say rusticula or rustica for perdix rustica [wild partridge]. This is taken from the Greeks, for whom ἡ ἄγρια πέρδιξ [hē agria perdix] is the same as ὁ σκολόπαξ [ho skolopax]. So Herodian defines it. Therefore πέρδιξ [perdix] could have been put by the Greek translators for the skolopax; especially since the Greek σκολόπαξ [skolopax] is little used and occurs nowhere except in two passages of Aristotle ^{q)}, from which it was taken by Hesychius and Herodian. Hence, [II, 645] if instead of ἐφώνησε πέρδιξ [ephōnēse perdix] the Greeks had written ἐφώνησε σκολόπαξ [ephōnēse skolopax], many would have stumbled at this word, struck by its novelty ^{(6)}.
